questions.text: Why should an LLM evaluation rubric anchor each score to observable behavior?

options.A: It guarantees that the judge cannot make factual mistakes.
options.B: It removes the need for representative evaluation examples.
options.C: It ensures every prompt revision receives a higher score.
options.D: It reduces ambiguity about what each score means for the judge.

questions.explanation: Behavioral anchors give the judge concrete criteria and reduce scoring ambiguity; calibration and representative data remain necessary.

questions.text: A prompt change reduces hallucinations but also causes many useful answers to become refusals. Which evaluation design best exposes this tradeoff?

options.A: Compare only hallucination rates on five handpicked examples.
options.B: Score correctness and helpfulness on the same representative cases for both versions.
options.C: Evaluate the new prompt only on examples included in its demonstrations.
options.D: Replace the baseline whenever the new prompt produces one impressive response.

questions.explanation: Before/after evaluation on shared representative cases with multiple criteria can reveal improved correctness alongside degraded helpfulness.

questions.text: compare_eval_runs marks a criterion REGRESSION only when diff < -0.3, otherwise STABLE unless diff > 0.3. ship_decision is SHIP if there are no regressions. For diff=-0.2 on every criterion, what does it report?

options.A: All criteria STABLE and SHIP, without using confidence intervals in that decision.
options.B: All criteria REGRESSION and BLOCK, because any negative difference blocks.
options.C: All criteria STABLE and BLOCK, because confidence intervals are always required.
options.D: All criteria IMPROVED and SHIP, because a negative difference favors the new version.

questions.explanation: The fixed threshold controls the status and deployment label. Confidence intervals are computed for reporting but do not determine the decision; SHIP does not establish statistical equivalence.
